site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Sama and the Arrow's Gentle Turn
stories.source: Sama Jataka, The Jataka, vol. VI, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: In a quiet forest, Sama the Bodhisatta fetched water for his blind parents until King Piliyakkha, mistaking him for game, let fly an arrow that struck him down. When the king realized he had wounded the devoted son who cared for two helpless elders, grief and shame flooded his heart.

Sama's parents did not cry for vengeance but spoke with quiet compassion, and a goddess moved through the wound, restoring Sama to health. From his place on the mossy ground, the Bodhisatta gently taught the king about the weight of every life and the duty of rulers.

Piliyakkha bowed for forgiveness, carried Sama safely back to his parents beneath the forest canopy, and rode home with softer hands. He vowed to govern with the same kindness he had finally learned from a son's arrow and a family's grace.

stories.title: The Monk Who Came Home
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: A learned monk, master of the art of spirit-roaming, wandered a forest path and found the still form of a dead king. Summoning his magic, he slipped free of his own body and entered the royal one, feeling breath and heartbeat return. The kingdom, overjoyed, hailed him as their new ruler.

His companion, watching the monk's empty body lie unguarded, could not resist. He stepped into the discarded frame and claimed it for his own, hoping to live as the wandering sage. But the king-monk, wise in the old dharmic ways, ruled with such patience and clear judgment that no one suspected the truth hidden beneath the crown.

In time, through careful discernment, the monk saw through his companion's trick and gently restored each spirit to its rightful body. He shed the weight of kingship, bowed to the memory of the king, and returned to the quiet forest path, grateful beyond words for the simple freedom of his own true form.

stories.title: The Small Truth That Stilled the Flames
body: In the dry season, smoke crept toward a low nest where a young quail still waited beneath the brush, unable yet to fly. Its parents hurried off to seek safer ground, leaving the trembling chick alone as orange tongues licked the fallen leaves.

The little quail did not panic or flee; instead it softly spoke the truth of kindness it had learned from the wise, offering the same gentleness to the advancing fire. Its voice was small, but steady, shaped by memory rather than fear.

Gently, the flames drew back from the nest, as if hearing an old, familiar kindness, and the unharmed chick blinked in the clearing smoke. In that quiet moment, the forest learned again that quiet courage, rooted in care, can turn even fire away.

stories.title: The Little Quail's Truth
stories.source: Vattaka Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: When flames raced through the forest toward a small nest, the young quail was still too small to fly. Its parents fled with the other birds, but the chick stayed behind, trembling in the dry brush.

Knowing it could not run, the little quail remembered the care of its mother and father, and the innocence of its own heart. Standing firm in the burning wood, it spoke gently to the fire, asking it to turn away.
The blaze, moved by the truth of the quail's words, parted around the nest and left a circle of cool earth untouched. The chick stood safe within it, and the forest fire passed on without harm.

stories.title: The Earrings Returned Home
stories.source: Mahabharata — Adi Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
body: When Uttanka finished his years of study with the sage Veda, he humbly asked what gift he might bring. The teacher's wife longed for the gleaming earrings of Queen Paushya, and Uttanka set out at once to honor her wish.

But the serpent king Takshaka snatched the jewels while Uttanka rested. Undeterred, the devoted student chased the thief into the hidden realm of the nagas, calling on divine aid until he stood before Takshaka and reclaimed what had been taken.

With the earrings safely in hand, Uttanka hurried back and presented them to his teacher's wife. Veda smiled upon his faithful pupil, blessing him for perseverance and reverence. A student's promise, kept through courage, became a quiet blessing for them both.
